[4] The Applicant’s refugee claim was rejected by the Refugee Protection Division on the basis that the Applicant was not credible and there was insufficient credible and consistent evidence to establish his claim. By decision dated March 3, 2025, the Refugee Appeal Division dismissed the Applicant’s appeal of the RPD’s decision, finding that the RPD was correct in finding that the Applicant was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The determinative issue was the Applicant’s credibility.

[5] While the RAD found that the RPD made some errors in the assessment of the Applicant’s credibility, the RAD ultimately agreed that the Applicant was not credible. The RAD concluded that the event at the core of the Applicant’s claim is his alleged treatment of the sexual assault patient. The RAD concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, the Applicant had not treated a sexual assault victim on the day in question and that everything that flowed from this allegation was also not true. The RAD’s conclusion was based on its determination that: (a) the Applicant’s description of the victim’s injuries was inconsistent; and (b) the Applicant’s description of the treatment provided to the victim was vague and inconsistent. The RAD stated that these determinations undermined the Applicant’s credibility. The RAD also found that the Applicant had failed to adequately explain omissions in his Basis of Claim form of visits from the police to his home many months later, which caused the RAD to draw a negative credibility inference.

[6] In assessing whether the RAD’s decision is reasonable, the Court will assess whether the decision is appropriately justified, transparent and intelligible. To meet these requirements, the decision must reflect “an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis” and be “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker.” Both the outcome and the reasoning process must be reasonable [Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 83, 85, 99].

[7] The Applicant asserts that the RAD made several errors in its assessment of his credibility. I agree, as the RAD’s determinations were unintelligible, lacking in transparency and failed to properly take into account the evidence before them.

[8] First, the RAD found that the Applicant’s description of the victim’s injuries was inconsistent, stating that there was a sufficiently marked difference between the description in the BOC (that the patient was “beaten nearly to death”) and the Applicant’s testimony (that the patient had scratches over her head and neck and a severe hematoma on her head). The RAD found that, as a trained medical professional, the Applicant should have been able to consistently describe her injuries.

[9] I find that the RAD failed to grapple with the Applicant’s evidence before the RPD where he explained how his description of the injuries was, in fact, consistent. The Applicant testified that the patient presented with a level 3 hematoma, which is the most serious kind. If the hematoma were to rupture, he stated, it could cause problems with the victim’s brain. There is no reference to this evidence in the RAD’s reasons, nor any rationale provided in the RAD’s reasons, as to how this evidence is inconsistent with the Applicant’s assessment of the patient’s injuries as reflected in his BOC.

[16] At the RPD hearing, the Appellant testified that when the patient arrived, there was no doctor. However, shortly after that, when asked by the RPD who took over the patient’s treatment, the Appellant stated that he provided her with first aid and that the doctor is the one who takes care of the patients. He went on to say that he was not present for the doctor’s treatment. Shortly after that, the Appellant then stated that the doctor was not there. On the second day of the RPD hearing, the Appellant testified that he examined the patient first, then called the doctors to examine. I find that the Appellant’s testimony regarding whether a doctor treated the patient is inconsistent and that the Appellant provided no explanation for this inconsistency.
[Footnotes omitted.]

[13] I find that the RAD’s reasons are illogical. The testimony cited by the RAD reveals no inconsistency in the Applicant’s evidence. A doctor was not present when the patient arrived. A doctor subsequently arrived (after being called by the Applicant and after the Applicant administered first aid) and took over the patient’s treatment.

[14] The aforementioned shortcomings in the RAD’s decision are a sufficient basis upon which to find the RAD’s decision unreasonable. As such, I need not go on to consider the balance of the Applicant’s arguments.

REASONS AND JUDGMENT

[1] The Applicant, a citizen of Kazakhstan of Tajik ethnicity, applied for refugee protection in Canada fearing persecution by the Zhetisai police due to his ethnicity.

[2] The Applicant, who is a paramedic, stated that a young girl was admitted to his clinic after being sexually assaulted. After treating the patient pursuant to the clinic’s protocol before transferring her care to the doctor, the Applicant stated he was told by the head of the clinic and a police officer not to report the incident nor to classify the patient’s injuries as a sexual assault. The Applicant states that he learned that the perpetrators of the assault were sons of municipal politicians in Zhetisai. The Applicant nonetheless reported the sexual assault and was fired from the clinic.

[3] The Applicant states that, the next day, two policemen visited the Applicant and claimed that he had been stealing drugs from the clinic and that he was being criminally charged. The Applicant states that, knowing the charges were fabricated, he fled and began his journey to Canada. Since arriving in Canada, he states that his family reports being surveyed and receiving visits at their home by the police.

[4] The Applicant’s refugee claim was rejected by the Refugee Protection Division on the basis that the Applicant was not credible and there was insufficient credible and consistent evidence to establish his claim. By decision dated March 3, 2025, the Refugee Appeal Division dismissed the Applicant’s appeal of the RPD’s decision, finding that the RPD was correct in finding that the Applicant was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The determinative issue was the Applicant’s credibility.

[5] While the RAD found that the RPD made some errors in the assessment of the Applicant’s credibility, the RAD ultimately agreed that the Applicant was not credible. The RAD concluded that the event at the core of the Applicant’s claim is his alleged treatment of the sexual assault patient. The RAD concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, the Applicant had not treated a sexual assault victim on the day in question and that everything that flowed from this allegation was also not true. The RAD’s conclusion was based on its determination that: (a) the Applicant’s description of the victim’s injuries was inconsistent; and (b) the Applicant’s description of the treatment provided to the victim was vague and inconsistent. The RAD stated that these determinations undermined the Applicant’s credibility. The RAD also found that the Applicant had failed to adequately explain omissions in his Basis of Claim form of visits from the police to his home many months later, which caused the RAD to draw a negative credibility inference.

[6] In assessing whether the RAD’s decision is reasonable, the Court will assess whether the decision is appropriately justified, transparent and intelligible. To meet these requirements, the decision must reflect “an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis” and be “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker.” Both the outcome and the reasoning process must be reasonable [Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 83, 85, 99].

[7] The Applicant asserts that the RAD made several errors in its assessment of his credibility. I agree, as the RAD’s determinations were unintelligible, lacking in transparency and failed to properly take into account the evidence before them.

[8] First, the RAD found that the Applicant’s description of the victim’s injuries was inconsistent, stating that there was a sufficiently marked difference between the description in the BOC (that the patient was “beaten nearly to death”) and the Applicant’s testimony (that the patient had scratches over her head and neck and a severe hematoma on her head). The RAD found that, as a trained medical professional, the Applicant should have been able to consistently describe her injuries.

[9] I find that the RAD failed to grapple with the Applicant’s evidence before the RPD where he explained how his description of the injuries was, in fact, consistent. The Applicant testified that the patient presented with a level 3 hematoma, which is the most serious kind. If the hematoma were to rupture, he stated, it could cause problems with the victim’s brain. There is no reference to this evidence in the RAD’s reasons, nor any rationale provided in the RAD’s reasons, as to how this evidence is inconsistent with the Applicant’s assessment of the patient’s injuries as reflected in his BOC.

[10] Second, the RAD found that the Applicant’s description of the treatment provided to the victim was vague and inconsistent. This finding was based on two considerations: (i) the RAD would have expected the Applicant to “systematically and logically describe the treatment that he and the others provided to the victim,” which the RAD claims he failed to do; and (ii) the Applicant gave inconsistent evidence regarding whether a doctor treated the patient.

[11] In relation to the first consideration, I find that the RAD’s reasons lack transparency, as the RAD does not explain how it reached its conclusion that the Applicant failed to provide sufficient evidence regarding the treatment of the victim. The RAD’s conclusion is particularly troubling given the Applicant had testified before the RPD regarding the treatment that he administered to the patient before the doctor took over her care. He stated that he assessed the patient’s blood pressure, administered magnesium and novocaine and conducted a preliminary examination of her injuries. There is no reference to any of this evidence in the RAD’s reasons, yet alone an explanation as to how this evidence regarding the patient’s treatment was insufficient.

[12] In relation to the second consideration, the RAD’s reasons provide:

[16] At the RPD hearing, the Appellant testified that when the patient arrived, there was no doctor. However, shortly after that, when asked by the RPD who took over the patient’s treatment, the Appellant stated that he provided her with first aid and that the doctor is the one who takes care of the patients. He went on to say that he was not present for the doctor’s treatment. Shortly after that, the Appellant then stated that the doctor was not there. On the second day of the RPD hearing, the Appellant testified that he examined the patient first, then called the doctors to examine. I find that the Appellant’s testimony regarding whether a doctor treated the patient is inconsistent and that the Appellant provided no explanation for this inconsistency.
[Footnotes omitted.]

[13] I find that the RAD’s reasons are illogical. The testimony cited by the RAD reveals no inconsistency in the Applicant’s evidence. A doctor was not present when the patient arrived. A doctor subsequently arrived (after being called by the Applicant and after the Applicant administered first aid) and took over the patient’s treatment.

[14] The aforementioned shortcomings in the RAD’s decision are a sufficient basis upon which to find the RAD’s decision unreasonable. As such, I need not go on to consider the balance of the Applicant’s arguments.

However, shortly after that, when asked by the RPD who took over the patient’s treatment, the Appellant stated that he provided her with first aid and that the doctor is the one who takes care of the patients. He went on to say that he was not present for the doctor’s treatment. Shortly after that, the Appellant then stated that the doctor was not there. On the second day of the RPD hearing, the Appellant testified that he examined the patient first, then called the doctors to examine. I find that the Appellant’s testimony regarding whether a doctor treated the patient is inconsistent and that the Appellant provided no explanation for this inconsistency.
[Footnotes omitted.]

[13] I find that the RAD’s reasons are illogical. The testimony cited by the RAD reveals no inconsistency in the Applicant’s evidence. A doctor was not present when the patient arrived. A doctor subsequently arrived (after being called by the Applicant and after the Applicant administered first aid) and took over the patient’s treatment.

[14] The aforementioned shortcomings in the RAD’s decision are a sufficient basis upon which to find the RAD’s decision unreasonable. As such, I need not go on to consider the balance of the Applicant’s arguments.

[15] In light of the RAD’s flawed assessment of the Applicant’s credibility, the application for judicial review shall be granted. The RAD’s decision shall be set aside and the appeal shall be remitted to a differently constituted panel of the RAD for redetermination.
[16] Neither party proposed a question for certification and I agree that none arises.

JUDGMENT in IMM-7220-25
THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that:
The application for judicial review is granted, the decision of the Refugee Appeal Division is set aside and the matter is remitted to a differently constituted panel of the Refugee Appeal Division for redetermination.
The parties proposed no question for certification and none arises.
